definition: A miniature plastic or metal fish with treble hooks, reeled with just the right jerk to look like a scared meal. Floating or sinking depending on weather, tide, and target.
The last few feet of line: heavier or clearer than the main line, with the lure or hook, often a swivel and a small weight above it. Matt adds a thirty-pound leader the night before the big snook.
A tiny metal figure-eight that joins main line to leader and keeps the line from twisting.
Dan's black-and-silver mullet imitation that 'glistens in the moonlight.' The lure that caught the South Point snook.
A feathered jig with a piece of shrimp on the hook; jigged over grass for trout, bounced for snapper.
A float with a cupped top; tug every few seconds and it 'pops' to call fish to the shrimp dangling beneath. How Matt caught his first snook and most redfish.
A curved metal flasher that wobbles on the retrieve. Matt's first post-storm cast.
Matt's prized red mullet lure with gold flecks.
Heavy rods with woven 30-lb test, steel tip leaders, and forged hooks for beach-casting at tarpon and sharks.
Wire leader that toothy fish can't bite through.
Line strength rated to hold thirty pounds before breaking.
A big hook on a pole for lifting a fish aboard by the mouth. Snapper's one lucky pass.
Long wooden pole for moving a boat silently through the shallows — how Snapper gets the Mako into the mangroves unheard.
Aluminum pipes hammered into the beach to hold rods after a long cast.
The universal Everglades bait, kept alive in a bucket with a battery aerator.
Battery-powered bubbler that keeps bait shrimp alive overnight.
Snapper tosses a small live snapper into the current and hooks the giant.
Letting the boat move with the tide and wind while casting. 'Drifting actually meant casting.'
Dragging a lure a hundred feet behind a moving boat. Little effort, long waits, then Old Scarface.
The upward yank at exactly the right bite. Too early and the hook flies out empty — Ch. 4.
A big fish moving just under the surface, pushing a ripple like a tiny boat.
Hold it upright and move it back and forth so water passes over the gills until the tail kicks. Done for the snook and for Old Scarface.
Fish the hour either side of high tide; 'morning high' means plenty of water over the oyster bars. Dan: the water isn't rising, the earth is turning through bulges of water pulled by sun and moon.
Seatrout hold over seagrass; mangroves and oysters hold snook and reds.
Snook spawn May–September; the book's Gulf-coast season is closed then and all snook go back.
Bow rope to one mangrove, stern anchor out — the boat 'stretched secure from end to end.'
How Dan reaches the Sea Belle.
The international hailing and distress channel. Dan says to leave it open 9–10 p.m.
Paper chart of the backcountry; cell reception is unreliable so 'they had to rely on actual maps.'
Swiveled over the bow to find Doc in the dark.
Matt's dolphin-rescue kit.
Novocain, needles, thread, antiseptic, gauze — and Matt's first stitches.
Peanut butter, three loaves of bread, cereal, cans, meat, milk, eggs, butter — 'a week of solid eating for two.' Plus donuts.
Tarpon, cobia, snapper, trout, drum — by weight. Snook, grouper, and redfish excluded under catch-and-release rules.
